title: How few rollouts can a capped certification test need while keeping both errors at 5%, and how far is the tuned SPRT from that optimum?
lede: Follow-up to free-sprtcut: backward induction gives the optimal capped test, 98.9 rollouts on average for 1% vs 5% at a cap of 181 (proved within 0.2% by a dual bound), against 107.3 for the grid-tuned SPRT and 181 for the fixed test; the tuned SPRT is 3 to 9% above the optimum at every cap tried.
summary: free-sprtcut re-tuned a capped SPRT on a coarse grid and listed “a backward-induction optimal truncated design” as the way to see how much was left. This project computes it. For multipliers c0, c1 the Bayes test minimising Ep0[N] + Ep1[N] + c0Pp0(accept) + c1Pp1(reject) is found exactly by backward induction over (rollouts, failures). Any test holding both errors at 5% costs at least that value minus 0.05(c0 + c1), a lower bound valid for every test including randomised ones; the best deterministic Bayes rule that holds both errors is the upper bound. For p1 = 1% against p0 = 5% (fixed test 181 rollouts) the optimal mean is 98.8–98.9 at a cap of 181, 94 at 1.1×, 88 at 1.5× and 87 at 2× and beyond; the bounds are within 1.1% of each other in all 21 cases (three (p0, p1) pairs, caps 1–3× the fixed size). The grid-tuned SPRT of free-sprtcut is 3–9% above the optimum in every comparable case (107.3 against 98.9 at 1×), and the optimum is roughly half the fixed test for 5% vs 1% and 10% vs 5%. Rollouts are assumed iid Bernoulli with the twin’s failure rate (no sim-to-real gap), the objective is the average of the two means only, the multiplier search is a local pattern search (the bounds, not the search, are what is certified), and nothing is sampled: every number is exact.
